title: Pauri 28, sound: mundaa santokh

segments.voice: Yesterday, the house where all sing. Your line was everything is singing. Did one annoying sound become part of the choir? Today, a new stretch of Japji, and some new people in it. Day two hundred nine.

Picture a group of wandering holy men in Guru Nanak's time. Hair matted, bodies smeared with ash, a patched coat, a begging bag over the shoulder, and in their ears, big rings, pushed through a split in the cartilage. These were the Nath yogis, famous across north India for their discipline and their power. Everyone knew them on sight by their outfit. Tradition says Guru Nanak met and talked with yogis like these more than once. The next four stanzas of Japji speak to them, in their own language. Today, the first line, and its sound.
screen: `WANDERING YOGIS, ASH AND EARRINGS.` → `KNOWN ON SIGHT BY THE OUTFIT.` → `JAPJI SPEAKS TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 28 in the original: mundaa santokh saram pat jholee dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot. Let's take the words one by one. Mundaa, MOON-daa: earrings, the large rings of the yogi. Santokh, sun-TOKH: contentment. You know it; it was our word on day one hundred eighty, enough, by listening. Saram, SUH-rum: effort, or modesty; commentators read it both ways. Pat: honor, the word from Pauri 14, going forth with honor. Jholee, JHO-lee: the pouch or begging bag the yogi carries. Dhiaan: meditation, attention. Bibhoot, bi-BHOOT: the ashes the yogis smeared on their bodies. So the line is built from pieces of the yogi's outfit, earrings, bag, ashes, each one paired with an inner quality. We'll open what that pairing means tomorrow. Today, notice the craft. Guru Nanak doesn't argue with the yogis in abstract terms. He picks up the very objects they carry and speaks through them. And one more sound to listen for. Each of these four stanzas, 28 to 31, ends with the same words: aades tisai aades. Aades was the greeting the Nath yogis used with each other. So Guru Nanak even closes in their greeting, and turns it: salutation to Him, salutation to the One. Say the first two words and you have today's carry. Mundaa santokh. Earrings, contentment. The outfit, and what it could mean.
screen: `MUNDAA — THE YOGI'S EARRINGS.` · `SANTOKH, SARAM, PAT, DHIAAN.` · `THE OUTFIT, PIECE BY PIECE.` · `AADES — THE YOGIS' GREETING.` · then, large: `MUNDAA SANTOKH.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: mundaa santokh, saram pat jholee, dhiaan kee karahi bibhoot. Slowly, letting each piece land. Say it again, a little quieter. Then, a third time, only the first two words: mundaa santokh. Then sit, and let the word santokh, contentment, rest where earrings would rest, close to your ears, close to what you hear. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 28. It opens mundaa santokh: earrings of contentment, a bag of effort and honor, ashes of meditation. Guru Nanak speaks to the yogis in their own things.
Your line: mundaa santokh. Today, when you put on something you wear every day, a ring, a watch, earrings, let it remind you of contentment. Day two hundred nine.

howItsDone: Pauri 28 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs know that pauris 28 to 31 are addressed to the yogis and end with aades tisai aades, salutation to Him.

original.note: Gurmukhi, Japji Pauri 28, line 1: earrings of contentment, a bag of effort and honor.

trapdoor: what you thought: a line about jewelry.
what it means: the yogi's earrings, bag and ashes, each turned into an inner quality: contentment, effort, honor, meditation.
what a scholar hears: the Nath yogis, called kanphatas for their split ears, greeted each other with aades; pauris 28 to 31 close with that greeting.
